title: Define the Book You Are Creating

content.text: Why do I need to write this book?
What experience do I want the reader to have?
What kind of reader is it for?
Is it entertainment, exploration, instruction, persuasion or some combination?
Is it a standalone book, a standalone with sequel potential, or part of a planned series?
For your epic fantasy, separate two promises:
1. Book One promise: What complete experience will this novel deliver?
2. Series promise: What larger transformation or conflict will unfold across the saga?
Adult epic fantasy with political conflict, ancient oaths, moral compromise and an ultimately hopeful resolution.
The North Star prevents the story from becoming an uncontrolled collection of ideas.
Beneath the fantasy conflict, it is really examining…
The reader should finish the book feeling…
Can someone use evil without becoming evil?
Is loyalty still virtuous when the cause is corrupt?
What does a person owe to a broken society?

gate: Do not begin detailed plotting until you can explain the intended book clearly in under one minute.

title: Find and Select the Core Idea

content.text: Do not demand that one idea carry the entire novel. Generate several categories of ideas.
A disgraced commander who must protect the people who condemned him.
A revolutionary who discovers that victory requires becoming what he hates.
A healer whose power transfers wounds rather than curing them.
The heir to a kingdom is murdered during peace negotiations.
An ancient treaty is discovered to have been deliberately mistranslated.
A magical barrier protecting humanity begins to fail.
Magic is created by binding promises.
Kingdoms are built over the remains of dead gods.
Memories can be inherited, traded or stolen.
Two morally defensible causes cannot coexist.
Saving one kingdom will condemn another.
The person destined to stop a prophecy is the one causing it.
A frozen battlefield where the dead remain standing.
A king receiving news of his son’s death before dawn.
A child carrying a forbidden book through a burning city.
Is a person responsible for evil committed under coercion?
Record every idea without judging it.
Strong stories often come from combining three or more elements:
Character + situation + world mechanism + moral problem.

A young oathkeeper discovers that the magical treaties holding the kingdoms together are built on an ancient lie. Exposing it could free the oppressed but also collapse the protections keeping an older enemy imprisoned.
Rate each potential idea from 1–5 for:
Ability to sustain a full novel
Choose the idea you would still want to explore after spending several years with it.
The story engine is the recurring source of movement and conflict.
A premise may sound interesting but still lack an engine.
A prince learns that his kingdom was founded on a lie.
After discovering that his kingdom was founded on a lie, a prince must find the surviving witnesses before his father’s secret police kill them.

gate: The idea must create continuous action, escalation and meaningful choices—not merely interesting history.

title: Build the Premise

content.text: When an initiating event happens, a specific protagonist must pursue a difficult objective, but an opposing force stands in the way, forcing the protagonist to confront the central moral or personal problem.

When an ancient oath protecting the northern kingdoms is broken, a disgraced royal guard must escort the suspected oathbreaker to the capital before civil war begins, while deciding whether the law he serves deserves to survive.
4. Opposition: Who or what prevents it?
5. Stakes: What happens if the protagonist fails?
6. Urgency: Why must this happen now?
7. Transformation: How will the struggle change the protagonist?
Expand the sentence into three paragraphs:
Who is the protagonist before the central conflict? What is wrong or incomplete in their life?
What happens, what goal emerges, and what stands in the way?
What choices, losses and revelations will force the protagonist to change?
Does the protagonist have to act?
Can success or failure be recognised?
Is there a credible opposing force?
Does the protagonist face difficult choices?
Could this sustain an entire book?
Does it promise the experience expected from the genre?
Does it contain emotional conflict as well as physical conflict?

gate: You should be able to generate at least ten major complications from the premise.

title: Establish Theme and Meaning

steps.title: Turn the theme into a question

content.text: Avoid beginning with a sermon or predetermined answer.
Can someone hold great power without being corrupted by it?
The story then tests possible answers through different characters.
Give major characters different responses to the thematic question.
Protagonist: Power can be controlled through good intentions.
Mentor: Power can only be controlled through discipline.
Antagonist: Power belongs to whoever can take it.
Ally: All concentrated power eventually becomes abusive.
Victim: Power is irrelevant unless ordinary people are protected.
Theme should appear through choices and consequences rather than speeches.
What does this decision reveal about the protagonist’s current answer to the theme?
The climax should contain the protagonist’s strongest thematic decision.

gate: The theme must affect the plot. Removing it should materially weaken the protagonist’s decisions.

title: Design the Series Before the Individual Book

content.text: What is wrong with the world at the beginning?
What hidden truth drives the larger conflict?
What force is changing or threatening the world?
Who benefits from the present system?
What must ultimately be defeated, restored, exposed or transformed?
How will the world be different at the end?
Describe the protagonist at four points:
1. At the beginning of Book One
2. At the first major series transformation
3. At the lowest moral or emotional point
4. At the conclusion of the series

steps.title: Give each book its own purpose

content.text: A primary antagonist or opposing force
A contribution to the larger saga
Book One should not feel like a 150,000-word introduction to Book Two.
Each book should escalate at least one dimension:
Record where it is introduced, developed and resolved.

intro.text: For a planned epic series, build the skeleton of the saga without outlining all nine books scene by scene.

gate: You know the broad destination of the saga, but Book One still functions as a satisfying novel.

title: Build the World Around the Story

content.text: Do not start by inventing thousands of years of history.
Geography should influence politics, food, war, trade, architecture and culture.
For each important realm or faction, define:
Who is protected by the system
What could cause the system to collapse
How ordinary people earn a living
How magic affects labour and wealth
Economic pressure frequently creates more believable conflict than invented hatred.
Concepts that lack direct equivalents in other cultures
Avoid making every member of a culture identical. Include regions, classes, generations, reformers and internal disagreements.
How beliefs affect law and morality
What happens when faith and evidence conflict
The most important question is not merely:
You do not need a complete chronology at first. Identify the past events still affecting the present:
Information needed to keep the story consistent.
Material that may become relevant in later books.

gate: The world creates obstacles and opportunities for the characters. It is not merely decoration.

title: Create the Characters

content.text: Want: What the protagonist consciously pursues.
Need: What the protagonist must learn, accept or become.
The want drives the plot. The need drives the character arc.
Courageous in battle but afraid of intimacy
Honest about facts but dishonest about motives
Loyal to individuals but hostile to institutions
Kind to strangers but cold toward family
The protagonist must cause major developments.
What decisions can only this character make?
What mistakes make the situation worse?
What risks do they voluntarily accept?
How do their actions alter the antagonist’s plans?
What happens because of their personality rather than coincidence?
A believable reason for wanting it
Personal or ideological connection to the protagonist
Something valuable or truthful in their position
The antagonist is not merely cruel. The antagonist is pursuing an outcome incompatible with the protagonist’s objective.
Every major supporting character should serve several purposes:
Avoid characters who exist only to provide exposition.
What each person wants from the other

6. The character recognises a deeper truth.

A negative arc follows a similar structure, but the character embraces a more destructive belief.
A flat arc involves a character who already holds an important truth and changes the world by defending it.

gate: Every major character wants something, fears something and can act independently of the protagonist.

content.text: You do not need every detail, but determine:
What decision resolves the internal arc?
What remains unresolved for the series?
The ending determines what must be prepared earlier.
Reveal the problem beneath the surface.
Force the protagonist into the story.
The protagonist crosses a threshold and cannot easily return to ordinary life.
The meaning of the conflict changes through a major victory, defeat, revelation or commitment.
The protagonist loses a major protection, assumption, relationship or advantage.
The protagonist faces the most difficult choice in the story.
The protagonist acts, and the central conflict is decided.
The consequences become visible and a new normal begins.

Not every beat needs its own chapter. Some require several chapters; others may occur within one scene.

Coincidence may create trouble. It should rarely solve trouble.

Where it intersects the main plot

content.text: A scene should change at least one important condition:
If nothing changes, the scene may be unnecessary.
A strong dramatic scene usually contains:
1. Situation: Where are we and what is happening?
2. Goal: What does the viewpoint character want now?
5. Choice: What must the character decide?

title: Establish the Narrative Method

content.text: What unique story access does each viewpoint provide?
Does each viewpoint have its own arc?
Do not give a character viewpoint status merely because they are present during an interesting event.
Choose past or present tense and remain consistent unless the narrative deliberately requires a change.
Decide how closely the narration follows the character’s mind.
Create a short style guide covering:
The reader would otherwise misunderstand the scene
Worldbuilding should usually enter through conflict, labour, customs, consequences and character assumptions—not lectures.

gate: You know how the story will sound, whose experience controls it and what information readers can access.

title: Write the First Draft

content.text: The first draft’s purpose is to discover and construct the complete story.
Do not try to perform developmental editing, line editing and proofreading while drafting.
When you find a problem, insert a note:
[CHECK TRAVEL TIME] [ESTABLISH THIS RULE EARLIER] [REWRITE AFTER ANTAGONIST MOTIVE IS FINALISED]
Enter close to the important action.
Instead of showing every arrival, greeting and meal, begin when:
The character makes a dangerous request.
Once the central change has occurred, leave before the scene loses energy.

steps.title: Update the outline when discoveries are structural

content.text: Do not force the draft to follow an obsolete outline.

gate: The story reaches its ending. Placeholders and weak scenes are acceptable; missing sections are not.

title: Diagnose Before Revising

content.text: Create some distance before major revision. The goal is to return as a reader rather than continuing as the drafter.
Read the complete manuscript and record reactions separately.

What it is trying to be
What must be protected during revision
Never polish sentences in a scene that may be deleted.

title: External Reader Testing

content.text: Do not rely only on people who want to encourage you.
Which character did you care about most?
Did the climax satisfy the story’s promises?
What did you expect to happen that never happened?
Do not obey every suggested solution.
If several readers say a scene is slow, the problem is probably real. Their proposed repairs may differ because they are diagnosing symptoms.

gate: Readers understand the intended story and generally experience the emotions you designed.
